I'm Damini, Devika's cousin, and I was holding the new baby at my brother's naming ceremony when it started. Devika, twenty-two, had just finished her first week as a lab assistant. Within minutes three relatives had found her. Mausi: "Next it's your wedding, na? Twenty-two is the right age." Chachaji: "Lab assistant? What's the salary? Your cousin in Pune gets double." An aunty: "Don't wait too long, beta."
I can't say what was going on in her head. I saw her fingers twist the end of her dupatta and her smile go stiff. Then she took a breath and said, "When it's right for me, Mausi, you'll be the first to know. And the lab work is exactly what I wanted." She said it gently and didn't argue. Afterwards she came and took the baby from me and held it for a long time.

qa.a: Her first week as a lab assistant.

qa.q: What do Devika's twisting fingers and stiff smile suggest?
qa.a: They suggest she felt uncomfortable and pressured, judged and rushed by the questions, though Damini can't be sure what she felt.

qa.q: What choice did Devika make at the turning point with Mausi?
qa.a: Instead of arguing or giving in, she said gently that she would share news when it's right for her and that she chose the lab work.

qa.q: How might Mausi see the questions compared with how Devika felt them?
qa.a: Mausi may think she is showing care by following the usual timetable, not realising the questions felt like pressure.

grounding: A cousin watches a young woman questioned about marriage and salary by relatives with a fixed timetable, who feels the pressure and answers kindly on her own terms.

Dear Imtiaz,
I'm leaving this on your desk because when we talk, I end up sounding like your Nani did with me.
When you moved back home in March, I told my friends you were "between things". I lay awake doing sums: at twenty-five I was married, working at the bank, with a baby on the way. You have changed jobs three times. I worried you were lost.
Then Rehana at work said her son's path looked just like yours, and she showed me an article saying most young people take longer to settle now. Maybe the road is simply longer than mine was.
So instead of a verdict, I have questions. What did you like in each job? What do you want the next one to have? And is there anything you need from me, other than silence at dinner?
With love and a little less worry,
Your Ammi, Ritu

qa.a: In March.

qa.q: How might Imtiaz feel finding questions on the desk instead of a lecture?
qa.a: Imtiaz may feel respected rather than judged, and more willing to talk than to sit in silence at dinner.

Vikas is twenty-six. Four jobs in three years: a bank, a startup that shut, a travel company, now something with maps. And still in the room with the cricket posters. Every Sunday I'd say, "At your age your father and I had a flat and a child." Every Sunday a door would bang.

I'm Joseph, and last year my son Divyansh, fourteen, went from telling me every cricket score to answering in single words. It hurt more than I expected.
At first I clung: I checked his phone and asked ten questions at dinner. He shut down further. Then I went the other way and sulked, stopped asking anything. The house went cold.
What finally worked was boring. Every evening at seven I walked our dog, and I asked if he wanted to come. Mostly he said no. I kept asking. The rules stayed the same: home by eight, phone off at ten.
In March, on a walk, he said, "I've been going to Nikhil's instead of tuition. I don't understand the maths and I was scared to tell you." I didn't shout. We found him a different tutor.
He still grunts sometimes. But he comes on the walks.

qa.a: At seven.

qa.a: He didn't understand the maths and feared his father's anger, so hiding it felt safer.
